points: Boot order: UEFI or BIOS, then GRUB2, then the kernel and initramfs, then systemd (PID 1), then the default target.
modprobe loads a module with its dependencies. insmod does not. lsmod lists loaded modules. modinfo describes one.
/proc and /sys are virtual filesystems built in memory. Runtime kernel settings live under /proc/sys and are set with sysctl.
Copyleft licences such as the GPL require derived work to keep the same licence.
learn.idea: A Linux system boots in stages: firmware, bootloader, kernel, then systemd. Knowing each stage tells you where to look when something breaks.
learn.memory: FBKS: Firmware, Bootloader, Kernel, Systemd.

questions.q: Which of the following filesystems contains non-persistent or volatile data?
questions.explain: /proc is a virtual filesystem the kernel builds in memory. Its contents describe processes and kernel state and are rebuilt every boot.

questions.q: Which command displays only the running kernel release?
questions.explain: uname -r prints just the release, such as 6.8.0-45-generic. uname -a prints everything.

questions.q: Which directory holds the kernel images, initramfs files and GRUB files?
questions.explain: The bootloader reads the kernel and initramfs from /boot.

questions.q: After editing /etc/default/grub on a RHEL system, which command applies the change to the boot menu?
questions.explain: grub2-mkconfig rebuilds grub.cfg from /etc/default/grub. grub2-install writes the bootloader to a disk, which is a different job.

questions.q: An administrator needs to load a kernel module and any modules it depends on. Which command should be used?
questions.explain: modprobe reads the dependency map and loads everything needed. insmod loads one file and ignores dependencies.

questions.q: Which command shows a kernel module's description, licence, author and accepted parameters?
questions.explain: modinfo reads the module's metadata. lsmod only lists what is loaded.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Put the Linux boot process in the correct order.
steps: Firmware (UEFI or BIOS) runs POST and finds a boot device
GRUB2 loads and shows the boot menu
The kernel and initramfs load into memory
questions.explain: Firmware hands off to the bootloader, the bootloader loads the kernel and initramfs, and the kernel starts systemd, which brings up the default target.

questions.q: A faulty driver module must never load at boot. What is the correct way to stop it?
options: Add a blacklist line for the module in a file under /etc/modprobe.d/
Run rmmod from a cron job every minute
Run lsmod -d with the module name
questions.explain: A blacklist entry in /etc/modprobe.d/ stops automatic loading. /proc/modules is generated by the kernel and cannot be edited.

questions.q: Match each directory to what it holds.
questions.explain: These come from the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard and show up often in questions.

questions.q: A server must forward IPv4 packets and keep that setting after a reboot. What should the administrator do?
options: Add net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1 to a file in /etc/sysctl.d/ and run sysctl --system
questions.explain: Writing to /proc/sys works only until reboot. A file in /etc/sysctl.d/ makes it persistent, and sysctl --system loads it now.

questions.q: Which software licence type requires anyone who distributes a modified version to release it under the same licence?
questions.explain: Copyleft licences such as the GPL keep derived work open. Permissive licences such as MIT do not require this.

questions.q: Which display server protocol is the modern replacement for the X Window System and is the default session on current GNOME desktops?
questions.explain: Wayland replaces X11. Xorg is the X server itself, VNC is remote desktop, and Mesa is a graphics library.

questions.q: A new storage driver must be available during early boot on a RHEL server. Which command rebuilds the initramfs?
questions.explain: dracut builds the initramfs on RHEL-family systems. Debian-family systems use update-initramfs.

points: LVM order: pvcreate, vgcreate, lvcreate, mkfs, mount.
lvextend -r grows the LV and the filesystem together. XFS can grow but cannot shrink.
Mount by UUID in /etc/fstab and test with mount -a before rebooting.
Software RAID uses mdadm. Check its health in /proc/mdstat.
learn.idea: Disks are split into partitions or LVM volumes, formatted with a filesystem, then mounted. LVM lets you grow storage without downtime.
learn.memory: P-V-L: Physical, Volume group, Logical. Build from the bottom up.

questions.q: HOTSPOT: A new disk /dev/sdc was added. Complete each command to give it a GPT label, create one 10 GB ext4 partition and format it.
questions.explain: mklabel writes the GPT partition table, mkpart creates the partition, mkfs.ext4 formats it, and lsblk -f confirms the result.

questions.q: SIMULATION: A junior administrator removed an LVM logical volume by mistake. Put the recovery steps in order.
questions.explain: Find the archive taken before the removal, restore the VG metadata from it, activate the LV, then mount it to reach the data.

questions.q: An administrator needs to extend the logical volume lv_data in volume group vg0 by 5 GiB and resize its ext4 filesystem in one step. Which command does this?
questions.explain: -r (--resizefs) grows the filesystem with the LV. resize2fs alone cannot make the LV bigger.

questions.q: Which is the correct field order for an entry in /etc/fstab?
options: device, mount point, filesystem type, options, dump, pass
mount point, device, options, filesystem type, pass, dump
device, filesystem type, mount point, dump, pass, options
device, options, mount point, filesystem type, dump, pass
questions.explain: The format is device, mount point, type, options, dump, fsck pass.

questions.q: After adding a new swap partition and its /etc/fstab entry, which command activates all swap entries from fstab?
questions.explain: swapon -a turns on every swap device listed in /etc/fstab.

questions.q: Which command creates a 10 GiB logical volume named lv_app in volume group vg_data?
questions.explain: The pattern is lvcreate -L size -n name vg.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Turn the new disk /dev/sdb into a 20 GB XFS volume mounted at /app. Put the commands in order.
questions.explain: Build LVM from the bottom up: physical volume, volume group, logical volume. Then format and mount.

questions.q: Which command lists block devices as a tree and shows each filesystem type and UUID?
questions.explain: lsblk -f shows disks, partitions and LVs as a tree with filesystem type, label and UUID.

questions.q: An XFS logical volume was extended with lvextend, but df still shows the old size. Which command grows the filesystem?
questions.explain: XFS is grown with xfs_growfs on the mounted path. resize2fs is for ext2, ext3 and ext4.

questions.q: An XFS filesystem can be shrunk with xfs_growfs to free space for another volume.
questions.explain: XFS can only grow. To shrink it, back up the data, recreate a smaller filesystem and restore.

questions.q: The volume group vg0 is full. A new disk /dev/sdd has been initialised with pvcreate. Which command adds it to vg0?
questions.explain: vgextend adds physical volumes to an existing volume group. vgcreate would try to make a new one.

questions.q: Which command prints the UUID of /dev/sdb1 so it can be used in /etc/fstab?
questions.explain: blkid reads the UUID from the filesystem. uuidgen makes a brand new random UUID.

questions.q: An administrator added a line to /etc/fstab. What is the safest way to test it before rebooting?
options: Run mount -a and check for errors
questions.explain: mount -a mounts everything in fstab that is not already mounted, so a typo shows up now instead of at the next boot.

questions.q: Which command creates a software RAID 1 mirror from /dev/sdb and /dev/sdc?
questions.explain: mdadm --create builds a new array. --assemble starts an existing one.

questions.q: Which file shows the live status of all Linux software RAID arrays, including rebuild progress?
questions.explain: /proc/mdstat shows each array, its members and any resync or rebuild in progress.

questions.q: A volume group has two 500 GiB physical volumes. One 600 GiB logical volume exists. How many GiB are still free in the volume group?
questions.explain: 500 + 500 = 1000 GiB total. 1000 minus 600 = 400 GiB free.

questions.q: Which command mounts the NFS export /exports/data from the server fileserver to /mnt/data?
questions.explain: NFS uses the server:/path form. The //server/share form is for SMB (cifs).

questions.q: Which command mounts the Samba share //files01/projects to /mnt/projects as user jdoe?
questions.explain: SMB shares are mounted with type cifs and the //server/share path. smbclient is an FTP-like client, not a mount tool.

questions.q: A hard link can point to a file on a different filesystem.
questions.explain: A hard link is another name for the same inode, and inode numbers only mean something within one filesystem. Use a symbolic link across filesystems.

points: ip addr, ip route and ip link show and change settings until the next reboot.
nmcli con mod changes a saved profile. nmcli con up applies it.
netplan try applies a change and rolls it back unless you confirm it.
/etc/hosts is checked before DNS when /etc/nsswitch.conf says files dns.
learn.idea: Linux networking is set with ip for quick changes, then made permanent with NetworkManager (nmcli) or netplan.
learn.memory: ip changes are pencil. nmcli and netplan are pen.

questions.q: An administrator updates the network configuration on a server but wants to make sure the change will not cause an outage if something goes wrong. Which command should be used?
questions.explain: netplan try applies the change and reverts on its own unless you confirm it, so a bad config cannot lock you out.

questions.q: Using NetworkManager, which command sets the static IPv4 address 192.168.10.50/24 with gateway 192.168.10.1 on the connection eth0?
options: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.50/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.10.1
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.static yes 192.168.10.50/24
ip addr add 192.168.10.50/24 dev eth0 permanent
questions.explain: nmcli con mod with ipv4.method manual plus addresses and gateway saves the profile. Bring it up again with nmcli con up eth0.

questions.q: Which command shows the IP addresses assigned to every interface?
questions.explain: ip addr (or ip a) lists each interface with its addresses. ip route shows the routing table.

questions.q: A server has no default route. Which command adds one through 192.168.1.1 until the next reboot?
questions.explain: ip route add default via gateway adds the route now. Save it in the connection profile to keep it.

questions.q: Which command sets the hostname to web01 so it survives a reboot?
questions.explain: hostnamectl writes /etc/hostname and updates the running name. The plain hostname command only lasts until reboot.

questions.q: Which file maps host names to IP addresses locally on one machine?
questions.explain: /etc/hosts holds static name-to-address entries. resolv.conf lists DNS servers.

questions.q: A server must check /etc/hosts before asking DNS. Which file controls that lookup order?
questions.explain: The hosts: line in /etc/nsswitch.conf, such as hosts: files dns, sets the order.

questions.q: On a system using systemd-resolved, which command shows the DNS servers in use for each interface?
questions.explain: resolvectl status lists the DNS servers and search domains per link.

questions.q: HOTSPOT: Match each NetworkManager task to the right command.
pairs: Show the state of each network device
Re-read connection files edited by hand
questions.explain: con works on saved profiles. dev works on the physical or virtual devices.

questions.q: Where does netplan read its configuration files from?
questions.explain: netplan reads YAML files in /etc/netplan/ and renders them for systemd-networkd or NetworkManager.

questions.q: Which command brings the interface eth1 up?
questions.explain: ip link changes the state of an interface. ip addr and ip route deal with addresses and routes.

questions.q: Two NICs are bonded on a server. Only one should carry traffic, and the other should take over if it fails. Which bonding mode fits?
questions.explain: active-backup keeps one link active and one on standby. 802.3ad needs switch support and uses both links.

questions.q: Which command shows the neighbour (ARP) table of IP-to-MAC mappings?
questions.explain: ip neigh replaces the older arp command and shows learned MAC addresses.

cards.front: Using NetworkManager, which command sets the static IPv4 address 192.168.10.50/24 with gateway 192.168.10.1 on the connection eth0?
cards.back: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.50/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.10.1

points: tar -c creates, -x extracts, -t lists. Add z for gzip, j for bzip2, J for xz.
rsync -av copies only changes. --delete makes the target an exact mirror.
find searches by name, time, size and permissions. xargs passes results to another command.
dd copies raw blocks. Check if= and of= twice before you press Enter.
learn.idea: Most admin work is moving, finding and archiving files. Learn tar, rsync, find and a few text tools well.
learn.memory: tar flags: Create, eXtract, lisT, and z-j-J for gz, bz2, xz.

questions.q: SIMULATION: An uncompressed backup of /opt/application is needed, and later a restore to the same place. Match each task to the command.
pairs: List the archive to check it
questions.explain: -C /opt stores the folder with a relative path, so extracting with -C /opt puts it back where it came from.

questions.q: /home/dev/web.bkp is a gzip-compressed tar archive. Which command extracts it into /var/www/html/?
questions.explain: gzip -dc decompresses to standard output and tar xf - reads the archive from the pipe in the current directory. tar -c would create an archive instead.

questions.q: Which command creates a gzip-compressed archive of /etc named etc.tar.gz?
questions.explain: c creates and z uses gzip. j would use bzip2 and x would extract.

questions.q: Which tar flag compresses the archive with xz?
questions.explain: J is xz, j is bzip2, z is gzip and x means extract.

questions.q: Match each compression tool to its usual file extension.
questions.explain: The extension tells you which tool, or which tar flag, to use.

questions.q: /srv/web/ must be mirrored to /backup/web/, and files deleted from the source must also be deleted from the copy. Which command does this?
questions.explain: --delete removes files from the target that no longer exist at the source. The second option copies in the wrong direction.

questions.q: Which command creates a full image of /dev/sda in /backup/sda.img?
questions.explain: if= is the input and of= is the output. Swapping them would overwrite the disk with the image file.

questions.q: Which command lists files under /var/www changed in the last 7 days?
questions.explain: -mtime -7 means modified less than 7 days ago. +7 means more than 7 days ago.

questions.q: Which pipeline prints each unique client IP from the first column of access.log?
questions.explain: uniq only removes duplicates that sit next to each other, so sort must come first.

questions.q: Which command deletes every .tmp file found under /tmp in one pipeline?
questions.explain: xargs turns the list from find into arguments for rm. rm does not read file names from standard input. (find -delete also works.)

questions.q: In vi or vim, which command saves the file and quits?
questions.explain: :wq writes and quits. :q! quits without saving and dd deletes a line.

questions.q: Which command extracts a cpio archive and creates directories as needed?
questions.explain: -i is copy-in (extract), -d makes directories and -v is verbose. -o creates an archive.

questions.q: A symbolic link keeps working after the file it points to is deleted.
questions.explain: A symbolic link stores a path. When the target is deleted, the link is left broken.

points: rpm and dpkg work on single package files. dnf and apt fetch from repos and solve dependencies.
Repos are defined in /etc/yum.repos.d/ (RHEL) and /etc/apt/sources.list.d/ (Debian).
Flatpak and Snap are distro-independent sandboxed formats.
From source: configure, make, make install.
learn.idea: Each distro family has its own package tools. RHEL uses rpm and dnf. Debian uses dpkg and apt.
learn.memory: Low level: rpm, dpkg. High level: dnf, apt.

questions.q: An administrator on a RHEL-family system must install the htop utility. Which command should be used?
questions.explain: RHEL 8 and later use dnf. apt is Debian-family, zypper is SUSE and pacman is Arch.

questions.q: Which command installs the local package file tool.deb on Ubuntu?
questions.explain: dpkg -i installs a .deb file. sudo apt install ./tool.deb also works and resolves dependencies.

questions.q: Which command shows which installed RPM package owns /usr/bin/ssh?
questions.explain: -qf queries by file. -ql lists the files inside a package you already know the name of.

questions.q: Which command lists every file installed by the Debian package nginx?
questions.explain: dpkg -L lists the files of a package. dpkg -S searches for the package that owns a file.

questions.q: Where should a new repository definition file be placed on a RHEL system?
questions.explain: dnf reads .repo files in /etc/yum.repos.d/. The apt path is for Debian systems.

questions.q: On Ubuntu, apt install says the package cannot be found, but it exists in the repo. What should be run first?
questions.explain: apt update refreshes the package lists. apt upgrade installs newer versions of what is already installed.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Put the steps to build and install software from a source tarball in order.
steps: Download and extract the source tarball
questions.explain: configure checks the system and writes the Makefile, make compiles, and make install copies the results into place.

questions.q: Which TWO are distribution-independent, sandboxed application package formats? (Choose two.)
questions.explain: Flatpak and Snap bundle apps with their dependencies and run on many distros. RPM and DEB are tied to their distro families.

questions.q: An administrator suspects system binaries were changed. Which command checks installed RPM files against the package database?
questions.explain: rpm -Va verifies size, checksum, permissions and owner of every installed file and reports changes.

points: virsh list --all shows running and stopped VMs.
qcow2 images support thin provisioning and snapshots. raw images are simple and fast.
Bridged networking puts VMs on the real LAN. NAT hides them behind the host.
Live migration needs compatible CPUs and the same shared storage path on both hosts.
learn.idea: KVM turns Linux into a hypervisor. libvirt manages it, with virsh on the command line and virt-manager as the GUI.
learn.memory: virsh for the shell, virt-manager for the mouse.

questions.q: To perform a live migration, which TWO must match on both host servers? (Choose two.)
questions.explain: The VM keeps running on the same CPU instruction set and must see its disk at the same shared storage path on the new host.

questions.q: Which command lists every libvirt virtual machine, including those that are shut off?
questions.explain: virsh list shows only running VMs. --all adds stopped ones.

questions.q: The VM web01 must start automatically whenever the KVM host boots. Which command sets this?
questions.explain: virsh autostart marks the domain to start with libvirtd. virsh start only starts it once.

questions.q: Which KVM disk image format supports thin provisioning and internal snapshots?
questions.explain: qcow2 grows as data is written and supports snapshots. raw is a plain block image.

questions.q: VMs must get IP addresses from the office DHCP server and appear as normal hosts on the LAN. Which network mode fits?
questions.explain: Bridged mode connects VMs straight to the physical network. NAT hides them behind the host's address.

questions.q: Which command checks whether the CPU supports hardware virtualization?
questions.explain: vmx is the Intel VT-x flag and svm is the AMD-V flag.

questions.q: Which graphical tool manages KVM virtual machines through libvirt?
questions.explain: virt-manager is the libvirt GUI. VirtualBox and vSphere are separate products.

points: enable sets start at boot. start runs it now. enable --now does both.
After editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload.
systemctl edit makes a drop-in override so package updates do not wipe your change.
mask blocks a unit completely. Timers (.timer units) can replace cron jobs.
learn.idea: systemd starts and watches services. Each service is a unit file, and systemctl is the remote control.
learn.memory: Edit, daemon-reload, restart. Every time.

questions.q: Which command enables the sshd service to start at boot and also starts it right now?
options: chkconfig sshd on && service sshd start
questions.explain: enable --now combines enable (start at boot) and start (start now).

questions.q: Which command checks whether the nginx service is set to start at boot?
questions.explain: is-enabled reports the boot setting. is-active reports whether it is running right now.

questions.q: An administrator edited /etc/systemd/system/app.service. What must be run before restarting the service?
questions.explain: daemon-reload makes systemd read changed unit files. Without it the old definition is still used.

questions.q: What is the best way to change one setting in a unit file shipped by a package so updates do not overwrite it?
options: Copy the file to /tmp and point systemd at it
questions.explain: systemctl edit creates a drop-in file under /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/ that overrides only what you change.

questions.q: A service must not be started by anyone, including other services that depend on it. Which command does this?
questions.explain: mask links the unit to /dev/null so it cannot start at all. disable only stops it starting at boot.

questions.q: A server should boot to a text console with networking instead of a desktop. Which command sets this?
questions.explain: multi-user.target is the normal non-graphical target. isolate changes the current state but not the default.

questions.q: HOTSPOT: Match each unit file directive to what it does.
pairs: The command that starts the service
Start this unit only after the named units
The target that pulls it in when enabled
questions.explain: ExecStart and Restart go in [Service]. After goes in [Unit]. WantedBy goes in [Install].

questions.q: Which systemd unit type can replace a cron job?
questions.explain: A .timer unit starts a matching .service unit on a schedule.

questions.q: Which command lists only the units that have failed?
questions.explain: systemctl --failed (or list-units --state=failed) shows every unit in the failed state.

questions.q: SIMULATION: A custom app needs to run as a service and start at boot. Put the steps in order.
steps: Check it with systemctl status app
questions.explain: Create the unit, let systemd read it, enable and start it, then confirm it is running.

questions.q: systemctl reload always stops and starts the service process.
questions.explain: reload asks the service to re-read its config without stopping, if the service supports it. restart stops and starts it.

questions.q: Which timer setting runs the matching service every day at 2:00 AM?
questions.explain: OnCalendar uses the year-month-day hour:minute:second format. The cron-style line is not valid in a timer.

points: useradd -m makes a home directory. -s sets the shell. Files from /etc/skel are copied in.
usermod -aG adds a supplementary group. Without -a the user is removed from other groups.
chage sets password age and account expiry.
getent reads users and groups from every source, including LDAP.
learn.idea: Every user has a line in /etc/passwd and a password hash in /etc/shadow. Groups give shared access.
learn.memory: -aG: Always Append Groups.

questions.q: An administrator needs to check the user ID, home directory and shell of the user accounting. Which command should be used?
questions.explain: getent passwd returns the full account entry, including UID, GID, home directory and shell. id shows only IDs and groups.

questions.q: A Linux administrator wants to add a user to the docker group without changing their primary group. Which command should be used?
questions.explain: -a appends and -G names a supplementary group. -g would change the primary group.

questions.q: Which command locks the account contractor by putting an exclamation mark in front of its password hash?
questions.explain: passwd -l locks the password. chage -l lists ageing info and passwd -S shows status.

questions.q: Which command forces the user dbadmin to change password every 90 days?
questions.explain: chage -M sets the maximum password age in days.

questions.q: Which command creates the user alice with a home directory and bash as her shell?
questions.explain: -m creates the home directory and -s sets the login shell. usermod changes an existing user.

questions.q: Which file stores user password hashes?
questions.explain: /etc/shadow holds hashes and is readable only by root. /etc/passwd shows an x in the password field.

questions.q: Every new user should get a standard .bashrc. Where should the administrator put it?
questions.explain: useradd -m copies everything in /etc/skel into the new home directory.

questions.q: Which command changes bob's login shell to /bin/zsh?
questions.explain: usermod -s changes the shell of an existing account. chsh -s /bin/zsh bob also works.

questions.q: An employee left. Which command removes their account and home directory?
questions.explain: userdel -r removes the home directory and mail spool too. Without -r the files stay.

questions.q: Match each field number in /etc/passwd to what it holds.
questions.explain: The fields are name, password placeholder, UID, GID, comment, home and shell.

questions.q: Which command creates a new group named developers?
questions.explain: groupadd makes the group. newgrp switches your current group for a session.

questions.q: Which TWO commands show the groups that dave belongs to? (Choose two.)
questions.explain: id lists UID, GID and groups. groups lists group names. who and last show sessions.

questions.q: A contractor's account must stop working on 31 December 2026. Which command sets this?
questions.explain: chage -E sets the account expiry date. -M sets maximum password age in days.

questions.q: On RHEL and Ubuntu, what is the first UID normally given to a regular (non-system) user?
questions.explain: UIDs below 1000 are reserved for system accounts. UID_MIN in /etc/login.defs sets this.

questions.q: Which command shows who is logged in and what each user is running?
questions.explain: w shows logged-in users and their current command. last shows login history.

points: kill sends signal 15 (TERM) by default. kill -9 forces it.
nice sets priority at start, renice changes it later. Higher nice means lower priority.
cron runs jobs on a schedule. at runs a job once.
Background jobs: command &, jobs, fg, bg. nohup keeps a job alive after logout.
learn.idea: Every program is a process with a PID. You can watch it, change its priority, signal it, or schedule it to run later.
learn.memory: Nice people go last: higher nice, lower priority.

questions.q: Which crontab line runs /opt/backup.sh at 2:00 AM every Sunday?
questions.explain: The fields are minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week. Day of week 0 (or 7) is Sunday.

questions.q: A process with PID 4321 ignores a normal kill. Which command forces it to stop?
questions.explain: Signal 9 (SIGKILL) cannot be caught or ignored. 15 is the polite default and 1 is hangup.

questions.q: A long report job should run with the lowest CPU priority. Which command starts it that way?
questions.explain: Nice 19 is the lowest priority. -20 is the highest and needs root.

questions.q: Which command lowers the priority of the running process 1234?
questions.explain: renice changes the nice value of a running process. nice only works when starting one.

questions.q: A command must run once tonight at 11 PM. Which tool fits best?
questions.explain: at schedules a one-time job. cron is for repeating jobs.

questions.q: A long copy must keep running after the administrator logs out of SSH. Which command fits?
questions.explain: nohup ignores the hangup signal sent at logout. A plain & job can be killed when the session ends.

questions.q: A job was sent to the background with &. Which command brings job 1 back to the foreground?
questions.explain: fg brings a job to the foreground. bg resumes a stopped job in the background.

questions.q: Match each signal to what it does.
pairs: Hangup, many daemons reload their config
Ends the process and cannot be caught
Asks the process to end cleanly
questions.explain: Try SIGTERM first so the program can clean up. Use SIGKILL only when it will not stop.

questions.q: A crontab entry starts with */15 * * * *. How many times does it run each hour?
questions.explain: */15 in the minute field means minutes 0, 15, 30 and 45.

questions.q: Which command prints the PIDs of every process named nginx?
questions.explain: pgrep finds PIDs by name. pkill sends a signal by name.

questions.q: Which command sends SIGTERM to every process named httpd?
questions.explain: pkill (or killall httpd) signals by name. kill needs a PID and killall -l only lists signal names.

points: journalctl -u unit, -b this boot, -p err priority, -f follow.
Make the journal persistent with /var/log/journal or Storage=persistent.
logrotate stops logs from filling the disk.
chrony keeps time in sync. timedatectl sets the time zone.
learn.idea: journald collects logs from the kernel and services. rsyslog can write them to files or send them to a central server. Accurate time keeps logs in order.
learn.memory: journalctl filters: u for unit, b for boot, p for priority, f for follow.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes journald?
options: A system service that collects and stores logging data
A feature that creates crash dumps if the kernel fails
A service that keeps the filesystem journal
A service that writes audit records to disk
questions.explain: systemd-journald gathers logs from the kernel, early boot and services into a structured journal.

questions.q: Which command follows new log entries for the nginx service in real time?
questions.explain: -u selects the unit and -f follows new entries.

questions.q: Which chrony command shows the configured NTP sources and their state?
questions.explain: chronyc sources asks the local chronyd for each source and how well it is reachable.

questions.q: Which command shows only error-level messages and worse since the current boot?
questions.explain: -b limits to this boot and -p err shows priority err and above.

questions.q: Journal logs disappear after each reboot. What makes them persistent?
options: Set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf (or create /var/log/journal) and restart journald
Run journalctl --flush every hour from cron
questions.explain: With volatile storage the journal lives in /run, which is cleared at boot. Persistent storage writes to /var/log/journal.

questions.q: Where should a custom rotation policy for an app's logs be placed?
questions.explain: logrotate reads its main file and every file in /etc/logrotate.d/.

questions.q: Which rsyslog rule sends all messages to 10.0.0.9 over TCP?
questions.explain: Two @ signs mean TCP. One @ means UDP.

questions.q: Which command sets the system time zone to America/Jamaica?
questions.explain: timedatectl manages time, time zone and NTP. localectl handles language and keyboard.

questions.q: Which command shows how much disk space the systemd journal is using?
questions.explain: --disk-usage reports the total. --vacuum-size removes old entries down to a size.

questions.q: A Bash script must write a message into the system log. Which command does this?
questions.explain: logger sends a message to the system logger, which journald and rsyslog then store.

questions.q: Which command shows how far the local clock is from its NTP source?
questions.explain: chronyc tracking shows the selected source, the offset and the frequency error.

cards.back: A system service that collects and stores logging data

points: docker run creates and starts. -d runs in the background, -p maps ports, -v mounts storage.
docker exec -it runs a shell in a container that is already running.
Podman runs containers without a daemon and can run rootless.
A Dockerfile starts with FROM. docker compose runs several containers from one file.
learn.idea: A container packs an app with what it needs and shares the host kernel. Images are templates. Containers are running copies.
learn.memory: run makes new. exec goes inside. logs tells you why it died.

questions.q: A Linux user needs to download the latest Debian image from a Docker registry. Which command does this?
questions.explain: pull downloads an image. Image names are lowercase, so debian, not Debian. save exports an image to a tar file.

questions.q: A Linux administrator needs to create and then connect to a container from app-01-image. Which command does this?
questions.explain: docker run creates and starts a container. -it gives an interactive terminal.

questions.q: Which command lists all containers on a Docker host, including stopped ones?
questions.explain: docker ps -a shows running and exited containers. docker images lists images.

questions.q: Which command starts an nginx container in the background, maps host port 8080 to container port 80, and names it web?
questions.explain: -d detaches, --name names it, and -p maps host:container.

questions.q: Which command builds an image tagged myapp:1.0 from the Dockerfile in the current directory?
questions.explain: docker build -t tag context. The dot uses the current directory.

questions.q: Which command opens a bash shell inside the running container web?
questions.explain: exec runs a new command in a running container. run would create a new container.

questions.q: A team wants to run containers without a root daemon and as normal users. Which tool fits?
options: Docker Engine with the default daemon
questions.explain: Podman is daemonless and supports rootless containers. Its commands match Docker's.

questions.q: A container must store its data in /srv/data on the host so the data survives when the container is removed. Which option does this?
questions.explain: -v host_path:container_path bind-mounts host storage. tmpfs lives in memory and is lost.

questions.q: A container exits right after starting. Which command shows its output to find out why?
questions.explain: docker logs shows what the container wrote to stdout and stderr.

questions.q: Which command removes images that no container uses?
questions.explain: prune removes dangling images. Add -a to remove every unused image.

questions.q: Which Dockerfile instruction sets the base image?
questions.explain: Every Dockerfile starts with FROM, for example FROM ubuntu:24.04.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Put these Dockerfile lines in a working order for an nginx image.
steps: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx
questions.explain: Start from a base, install software, copy in content, document the port, and set the default command last.

questions.q: Which command starts every service defined in compose.yaml in the background?
questions.explain: up creates and starts the services. -d detaches.

questions.q: Which command shows a container's full configuration, including its IP address and mounts?
questions.explain: docker inspect prints the full JSON configuration.

questions.q: The image app:1.0 was tagged as registry.example.com/app:1.0. Which command uploads it to that registry?
questions.explain: push uploads to a registry. pull downloads and save writes a local tar file.

points: r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. Add them per digit: 750 is rwxr-x---.
umask removes bits from new files (base 666) and directories (base 777).
SUID = 4, SGID = 2, sticky = 1 in front of the three digits.
setfacl gives one extra user or group access. chattr +i makes a file immutable.
learn.idea: Every file has an owner, a group and read, write and execute bits for owner, group and others. ACLs and special bits add finer control.
learn.memory: 4-2-1 for r-w-x. SUID-SGID-Sticky is also 4-2-1.

questions.q: Which command finds all files with the SUID bit set under /usr?
questions.explain: -perm -4000 matches any file that has the SUID bit, whatever its other bits are.

questions.q: Which chmod command sets SUID on a script and gives rwxr-xr-x to everyone else?
questions.explain: The leading 4 is SUID. 2 would be SGID, 1 sticky and 6 both SUID and SGID.

questions.q: What numeric mode gives rwxr-x--- (owner all, group read and execute, others nothing)?
questions.explain: Owner 4+2+1 = 7, group 4+1 = 5, others 0.

questions.q: The umask is 027. What numeric permissions does a newly created regular file get?
questions.explain: Files start from 666. Removing 027 gives 640 (rw-r-----).

questions.q: The user bob needs read access to report.txt without changing its owner or group. Which command does this?
questions.explain: setfacl -m adds an ACL entry for one user. chmod o+r would open it to everyone.

questions.q: Which command shows the ACL entries on a file?
questions.explain: getfacl prints the ACL. ls -l shows a + at the end of the mode when an ACL exists.

questions.q: In the shared folder /shared, users must only be able to delete their own files. What should be set?
questions.explain: The sticky bit lets only the file owner (or root) delete or rename files. /tmp uses it.

questions.q: What does the SGID bit do when it is set on a directory?
options: New files inside inherit the directory's group
Files run with the group owner's rights
Only the group owner can delete files
questions.explain: SGID on a directory keeps team folders owned by the team group.

questions.q: A config file must not be changed or deleted, even by root, until the flag is removed. Which command does this?
questions.explain: The immutable attribute blocks writes, renames and deletes, even for root, until chattr -i is run.

questions.q: Which command makes www-data the owner and group of /var/www and everything inside it?
questions.explain: chown -R changes owner and group recursively. chgrp alone changes only the group of one item.

questions.q: Match each chmod command to what it does.
questions.explain: u, g, o and a mean user, group, others and all. + adds, - removes and = sets exactly.

questions.q: In ls -l output, a capital S in the owner execute position means SUID is set but the owner has no execute permission.
questions.explain: Lowercase s means SUID plus execute. Capital S means SUID without execute, which is usually a mistake.

questions.q: What does the execute (x) permission allow on a directory?
options: Entering the directory and reaching files inside it
Running every script in the directory
Listing file names in the directory
Creating new files in the directory
questions.explain: x lets you cd into the directory and use paths through it. r lists names and w creates or deletes entries.

cards.back: New files inside inherit the directory's group

points: Set PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config once keys work.
~/.ssh must be 700 and authorized_keys 600 or sshd refuses the key.
Edit sudo rules with visudo. Put drop-in files in /etc/sudoers.d/.
pam_pwquality sets password strength. pam_faillock locks accounts after failed logins.
learn.idea: Control who can log in and what they can do. Use keys for SSH, sudo for admin rights, and PAM for password rules.
learn.memory: Test the key, then lock the door. Never disable passwords before a key login works.

questions.q: Which sshd_config directive stops direct root logins over SSH?
questions.explain: PermitRootLogin no blocks root. Admins log in as themselves and use sudo.

questions.q: Which command generates a modern Ed25519 SSH key pair?
questions.explain: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 creates the key pair. ssh-copy-id then installs the public key on a server.

questions.q: Which command must be used to edit the sudoers file safely with a syntax check?
questions.explain: visudo locks the file and checks syntax before saving, so a typo cannot break sudo.

questions.q: Which tool reads logs such as /var/log/auth.log and bans IP addresses with repeated failed logins through firewall rules?
questions.explain: fail2ban watches logs and adds temporary firewall bans for offending addresses.

questions.q: Which command installs your public key in the authorized_keys file on server01?
questions.explain: ssh-copy-id appends the public key to the remote authorized_keys with the right permissions. Never copy the private key.

questions.q: Key logins work for every admin. Which sshd_config setting now turns off password logins?
questions.explain: PasswordAuthentication no allows keys only. PubkeyAuthentication no would block the keys instead.

questions.q: Where should a new sudo rule for the backup team be placed so it survives package updates?
options: A new file in /etc/sudoers.d/, edited with visudo -f
questions.explain: Drop-in files in /etc/sudoers.d/ keep custom rules apart from the main file. visudo -f checks their syntax.

questions.q: Which sudoers line lets every member of the wheel group run any command as any user?
questions.explain: % marks a group. The format is who host=(runas) commands.

questions.q: Which PAM module enforces password length and complexity rules?
questions.explain: pam_pwquality checks new passwords against rules such as minlen and dcredit.

questions.q: Accounts must lock for 15 minutes after five failed logins. Which PAM module handles this?
questions.explain: pam_faillock counts failures and locks the account. faillock --user name --reset unlocks it.

questions.q: SSH key login fails with Permission denied (publickey). The key is in authorized_keys. Which permissions should be set?
questions.explain: With StrictModes on, sshd ignores keys if the folder or file is writable by others.

questions.q: An admin needs to reach a web app on port 80 that only listens on the server's localhost. Which command creates a tunnel from local port 8080?
questions.explain: -L forwards a local port to a destination as seen from the server. -R is a reverse tunnel and -D is a SOCKS proxy.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Move a server to key-only SSH logins without locking yourself out. Put the steps in order.
steps: Generate a key pair on your workstation with ssh-keygen
Copy the public key to the server with ssh-copy-id
Test a key login in a new terminal and keep the old session open
questions.explain: Prove the key works before you turn off passwords, and keep a working session open as a safety net.

questions.q: Which command joins a Linux server to an Active Directory domain using SSSD?
questions.explain: realm join discovers the domain, joins it and configures SSSD. kinit only gets a Kerberos ticket.

questions.q: Which command lists failed login attempts recorded on the system?
questions.explain: lastb reads /var/log/btmp, which records bad logins. last reads successful ones.

points: getenforce or sestatus shows the mode: enforcing, permissive or disabled.
ls -Z shows contexts. restorecon resets them to policy.
semanage fcontext makes a context rule permanent. setsebool -P makes a boolean permanent.
AppArmor uses path-based profiles. aa-complain logs without blocking.
learn.idea: SELinux and AppArmor add mandatory access control on top of normal permissions. A file can be 777 and still be blocked.
learn.memory: Check the context before you blame the permissions.

questions.q: An administrator must set SELinux to permissive mode for debugging without rebooting. Which command does this?
questions.explain: setenforce 0 switches to permissive until reboot. setenforce 1 goes back to enforcing.

questions.q: Which TWO commands show the current SELinux mode? (Choose two.)
questions.explain: getenforce prints the mode. sestatus prints the mode and more detail.

questions.q: Files copied into /var/www/html have the wrong SELinux context and the web server gets 403 errors. Which command fixes the contexts?
questions.explain: restorecon resets contexts to what the policy says that path should have.

questions.q: Web content lives in a custom folder /web. Which commands make the correct context stick, even after a relabel?
questions.explain: chcon changes are lost on relabel. semanage fcontext adds a lasting rule and restorecon applies it.

questions.q: The web server must connect to a remote database under SELinux, and the change must survive reboots. Which command does this?
questions.explain: -P writes the boolean to the policy so it persists. Without -P it lasts until reboot.

questions.q: nginx must listen on TCP 8443 on an SELinux enforcing system. Which command allows it?
questions.explain: SELinux only lets web servers bind to ports labelled http_port_t. Add the port to that type.

questions.q: Which command shows the SELinux context of files?
questions.explain: -Z adds the user:role:type:level context to the listing.

questions.q: An AppArmor profile is blocking nginx. The admin wants to log violations without blocking them while testing. Which command does this?
questions.explain: Complain mode logs what would be blocked. aa-enforce turns blocking back on.

questions.q: SIMULATION: A service fails only when SELinux is enforcing. Put the troubleshooting steps in order.
steps: Look for denials with ausearch -m avc -ts recent
Read the suggested cause with audit2why or sealert
Apply the fix with restorecon, setsebool or semanage
Retest the service in enforcing mode
questions.explain: Find the actual denial, understand it, fix the label, boolean or port, then test with SELinux still enforcing.

points: firewall-cmd changes are runtime only unless you add --permanent and reload.
Rules are checked top down. The first match wins.
ufw default deny incoming plus explicit allows is a solid baseline.
nft list ruleset shows everything nftables is doing.
learn.idea: A host firewall decides which traffic may reach the server. firewalld and ufw are friendly front ends. nftables and iptables are the engines.
learn.memory: firewalld: permanent, then reload, or it is gone.

questions.q: A web server is reachable on HTTP but HTTPS connections fail. Exhibit: $ ufw status → 443/tcp DENY Anywhere; 80/tcp ALLOW Anywhere | $ ss -tlnp → LISTEN 0.0.0.0:443 nginx. Which command best fixes this?
questions.explain: nginx is listening on 443 but a deny rule blocks it. Deleting that rule fixes it and keeps the firewall on.

questions.q: Which ufw commands build a firewall that blocks unsolicited inbound traffic but allows outbound traffic and inbound SSH?
options: ufw default deny incoming; ufw allow 22/tcp; ufw enable
ufw deny all in; ufw permit ssh
ufw policy drop; ufw enable ssh
ufw reject incoming && ufw allow OpenSSH && ufw on
questions.explain: Deny incoming by default, allow what you need, then enable.

questions.q: Which commands allow HTTPS permanently with firewalld and apply it now?
questions.explain: --permanent writes the rule to disk and --reload loads it into the running firewall.

questions.q: Which command shows every setting in the active firewalld zone?
questions.explain: --list-all shows interfaces, services, ports and rich rules for the zone.

questions.q: Which command prints the complete nftables configuration that is running?
questions.explain: nft list ruleset prints every table, chain and rule. flush would delete them all.

questions.q: Which iptables command drops all traffic from 203.0.113.5?
questions.explain: -A INPUT appends to the inbound chain, -s matches the source and -j DROP discards it.

questions.q: A port opened with firewall-cmd --add-port=8080/tcp, without --permanent, is lost after the firewall reloads or the server reboots.
questions.explain: Without --permanent only the runtime config changes.

questions.q: An admin appended an ACCEPT rule for port 22, but SSH is still blocked. iptables -L shows a DROP-all rule above it. What fixes it?
questions.explain: Rules are read top down and the first match wins. -I inserts the rule above the DROP.

questions.q: Match each command to the firewall it manages.
pairs: Uncomplicated Firewall on Debian and Ubuntu
questions.explain: Use the tool that matches the firewall service actually running on the host.

questions.q: The interface eth1 faces the trusted internal network. Which command permanently moves it to the internal zone?
options: nmcli con mod eth1 firewall internal-zone
ufw route allow in on eth1
questions.explain: --change-interface assigns the interface to the zone. Add --permanent so it survives reloads.

cards.front: Which ufw commands build a firewall that blocks unsolicited inbound traffic but allows outbound traffic and inbound SSH?
cards.back: ufw default deny incoming; ufw allow 22/tcp; ufw enable

Which command prints the complete nftables configuration that is running?
Which iptables command drops all traffic from 203.0.113.5?

cards.back: True. Without --permanent only the runtime config changes.

points: LUKS (cryptsetup) encrypts whole partitions. GPG encrypts files.
sha256sum creates and checks file checksums.
AIDE builds a baseline and reports changed files.
auditd records events. auditctl adds watch rules. ausearch finds them by key.
learn.idea: Encrypt data at rest, prove files have not changed, and record who did what.
learn.memory: Lock (LUKS), Seal (GPG), Check (sha256sum, AIDE), Watch (auditd).

questions.q: Which auditctl command watches /etc/passwd for writes and attribute changes and tags events with the key userdb?
questions.explain: -w sets the watch path, -p wa picks write and attribute changes, and -k sets a key for searching.

questions.q: Which command shows the TLS certificate presented by the web server at www.example.com?
questions.explain: s_client opens a TLS connection and prints the certificate chain. x509 -in reads a certificate file you already have.

questions.q: Which command sets up LUKS encryption on /dev/sdb1? (All data on it will be lost.)
questions.explain: luksFormat writes the LUKS header and sets the passphrase. open unlocks an existing LUKS device.

questions.q: Which command unlocks the LUKS partition /dev/sdb1 as /dev/mapper/securedata?
questions.explain: open maps the decrypted device under /dev/mapper. Then you mount that mapper device.

questions.q: Which command creates a SHA-256 checksum of an ISO file to compare with the vendor's value?
questions.explain: sha256sum prints the hash. Compare it with the published one, or check a list with sha256sum -c.

questions.q: Which command encrypts report.pdf so only alice@example.com can open it with her private key?
questions.explain: Encrypting to a recipient uses their public key. --sign proves who sent it but does not hide it.

questions.q: Which command creates a self-signed certificate and a new unencrypted private key, valid for 365 days?
questions.explain: req -x509 makes a self-signed certificate instead of a request. -nodes leaves the key without a passphrase.

questions.q: Which tool builds a database of file hashes and later reports which system files changed?
questions.explain: AIDE stores a baseline with aide --init and compares the system against it with aide --check.

questions.q: Which command finds audit events tagged with the key userdb?
questions.explain: ausearch -k searches the audit log by key. auditctl -l lists the loaded rules.

questions.q: A server runs a legacy service that nobody uses. What is the best hardening step?
options: Stop and disable the service, or remove its package
Leave it running but hide it from ss output
Give it a longer log retention
questions.explain: Fewer running services means less attack surface. Changing ports only hides it.

questions.q: Which algorithm is symmetric, using the same key to encrypt and decrypt?
questions.explain: AES is symmetric. RSA, Ed25519 and ECDSA use public and private key pairs.

points: Start with #!/bin/bash and make it executable with chmod +x.
$1, $2 are arguments, $# counts them, $@ is all of them, $? is the last exit code.
Quote variables: "$var". Use ${var} when text follows the name.
> overwrites, >> appends, 2> sends errors, 2>&1 joins errors to output.
learn.idea: A Bash script is a list of commands with variables, tests and loops. Small scripts save hours of repeated work.
learn.memory: $? is the question: did that last command work? 0 means yes.

questions.q: In a script, the line echo "profile-$num-$name" does not expand $num as expected. Which notation makes sure the value is expanded?
questions.explain: Braces mark exactly where the variable name ends. $(num) would try to run a command named num, and single quotes stop all expansion.

questions.q: Which line must begin an executable script so it always runs with Bash?
questions.explain: The shebang line names the interpreter. #!/usr/bin/env bash also works.

questions.q: In Bash, which special variable holds the number of arguments passed to a script?
questions.explain: $# is the count. $@ and $* are the arguments themselves and $0 is the script name.

questions.q: Which Bash test is true when /etc/hosts exists and is a regular file?
questions.explain: -f tests for a regular file. -d tests for a directory and -e for anything that exists.

questions.q: Which Bash loop prints the numbers 1 to 5, one per line?
options: for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done
loop i from 1 to 5; print i; end
questions.explain: Brace expansion {1..5} is the usual Bash way. for i in $(seq 1 5) also works.

questions.q: Which variable holds the exit status of the last command?
questions.explain: 0 means success and anything else means failure. $! is the PID of the last background job.

questions.q: A new script will not run and says Permission denied. Which command fixes it?
questions.explain: The file needs execute permission. bash -x runs it with tracing but does not fix the permission.

questions.q: Which line asks the user for a name and stores it in the variable name?
questions.explain: read stores a line from standard input in a variable. -p shows a prompt.

questions.q: Which line stores today's date in YYYY-MM-DD format in the variable today?
questions.explain: $( ) runs a command and captures its output. There must be no spaces around = in Bash.

questions.q: Which test checks whether the number in $count is greater than 10?
questions.explain: -gt compares integers. Inside [ ], > is treated as a redirect.

questions.q: Which keyword closes a case statement in Bash?
questions.explain: case closes with esac, if with fi, and loops with done.

questions.q: Which command sends only error messages from backup.sh to errors.log?
questions.explain: File descriptor 2 is standard error. 1 (or plain >) is standard output.

questions.q: Which command sends both normal output and errors from job.sh to job.log?
questions.explain: Redirect stdout to the file first, then point stderr at stdout. The other order sends errors to the terminal.

questions.q: Which loop reads servers.txt one line at a time into the variable line?
options: while read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < servers.txt
for line in read servers.txt; do echo $line; done
while servers.txt; do read line; done
questions.explain: Feed the file into the while loop with <. -r keeps backslashes as they are.

questions.q: What does set -e do near the top of a script?
options: Makes the script stop when a command fails
Prints each command before it runs
questions.explain: set -e exits on errors. set -x traces commands and set -u fails on unset variables.

questions.q: A script is run as ./backup.sh /data /mnt/usb daily. What is the value of $#?
questions.explain: There are three arguments: /data, /mnt/usb and daily. The script name is $0 and is not counted.

questions.q: A script sets BACKUP_DIR and then calls another script that must see it. What must be done?
questions.explain: export puts the variable in the environment of child processes. local limits it to a function.

questions.q: Which line correctly defines a Bash function named cleanup?
questions.explain: name() { commands; } is the standard form. The space after { and the ; before } are required on one line.

questions.q: Match each special variable to what it holds.
pairs: The PID of the current shell
questions.explain: Quote "$@" when passing arguments on, so names with spaces stay whole.

cards.front: In a script, the line echo "profile-$num-$name" does not expand $num as expected. Which notation makes sure the value is expanded?
Which line must begin an executable script so it always runs with Bash?
In Bash, which special variable holds the number of arguments passed to a script?
Which Bash test is true when /etc/hosts exists and is a regular file?
Which Bash loop prints the numbers 1 to 5, one per line?
cards.back: for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done

points: grep finds lines. -i ignores case, -r searches folders, -v inverts, -E uses extended regex.
sed 's/old/new/g' replaces text. -i edits the file in place.
awk -F sets the separator. $1, $2 are fields.
^ anchors the start of a line and $ the end.
learn.idea: sed, awk and grep turn raw logs and config files into exactly the lines you need.
learn.memory: grep finds, sed changes, awk reports.

questions.q: Which command replaces every "http://" with "https://" in site.conf, saving the change in the file?
questions.explain: -i edits in place and g replaces every match on a line. Any character can be the separator, which avoids escaping slashes.

questions.q: Which command prints the UID column (field 3) of /etc/passwd?
questions.explain: /etc/passwd uses colons, so -F: is needed. sed -n 3p prints line 3, not field 3. (cut -d: -f3 also works.)

questions.q: Which command searches every file under /var/log for "error" in any letter case?
questions.explain: -r searches folders and -i ignores case. -v would show lines without the word.

questions.q: Which command shows a config file without comment lines that start with #?
questions.explain: ^# matches lines that begin with # and -v hides them.

questions.q: Which lines does the regular expression ^root match?
options: Lines that do not contain root
questions.explain: ^ anchors to the start of the line. root$ would match the end.

questions.q: Which command prints only the usernames from /etc/passwd?
questions.explain: -d: sets the colon as the separator and -f1 takes the first field.

questions.q: Which command converts the text in names.txt to uppercase?
questions.explain: tr maps one set of characters to another. It reads standard input, so feed it the file.

questions.q: Which command shows lines in app.log that contain either WARN or ERROR?
questions.explain: -E turns on extended regex, where | means or.

questions.q: Match each tool to the job it does best.
pairs: Find and replace text in a stream or file
Pick out fields and build simple reports
Count repeated lines that sit together
questions.explain: Pipe them together, for example sort then uniq -c, to count occurrences.

points: The inventory lists hosts and groups. Playbooks are YAML lists of tasks.
Modules are idempotent: running twice gives the same result.
--check does a dry run. ansible-vault encrypts secrets. Handlers run only when notified.
Terraform builds infrastructure. cloud-init configures a new VM on first boot.
learn.idea: Configuration management describes how systems should look and applies it to many hosts the same way. Ansible does this over SSH with no agent.
learn.memory: Inventory says where. Playbook says what. Module says how.

questions.q: Which Ansible component contains a list of hosts and host groups?
questions.explain: The inventory tells Ansible which machines it manages and how they are grouped.

questions.q: Which Ansible ad-hoc command tests connectivity to every managed host with the ping module?
questions.explain: ansible pattern -m module. The pattern all matches every host in the inventory.

questions.q: Which ansible-playbook option does a dry run and reports what would change without changing anything?
questions.explain: --check runs in check mode. Add --diff to see the exact changes.

questions.q: In a playbook, which task correctly makes sure the nginx package is installed?
options: - name: Install nginx / apt: / name: nginx / state: present (each part on its own indented line)
questions.explain: A task is a list item with a name and a module, and the module's arguments sit indented under it.

questions.q: Which command runs site.yml only against hosts in the web group, using inventory.ini?
questions.explain: -i names the inventory and --limit narrows which hosts run.

questions.q: What does it mean that most Ansible modules are idempotent?
options: Running the same task again makes no further change once the system is in the right state
Each task runs only once and is then deleted
Tasks run on every host at the same moment
questions.explain: Idempotent tasks check the current state first, so repeat runs are safe.

questions.q: How does Ansible usually connect to Linux managed nodes?
options: Over SSH, with no agent installed on the nodes
Through an agent service on every node
Through a VPN client it installs
questions.explain: Ansible is agentless. Python on the node and SSH access are enough.

questions.q: Which command downloads roles and collections from the community hub?
questions.explain: ansible-galaxy installs roles and collections. ansible-doc shows module help.

questions.q: A playbook needs a database password that must not sit in Git as plain text. Which tool protects it?
questions.explain: ansible-vault encrypts variable files. Playbooks decrypt them at run time with the vault password.

questions.q: A playbook should restart nginx only when its config file actually changes. Which feature fits?
options: A fact gathered at the start
questions.explain: Handlers run only when a task reports a change and notifies them.

questions.q: Which tool creates cloud infrastructure such as networks and VMs from declarative code?
questions.explain: Terraform (or OpenTofu) is infrastructure as code. It plans changes and then applies them.

questions.q: Which configuration management tool normally relies on an agent installed on each managed node?
questions.explain: Puppet agents pull their config from a server. Ansible pushes over SSH with no agent.

questions.q: Which tool configures a new cloud VM on its first boot using user-data?
questions.explain: cloud-init reads user-data from the cloud platform to set users, keys, packages and scripts at first boot.

cards.front: Which Ansible component contains a list of hosts and host groups?
Which Ansible ad-hoc command tests connectivity to every managed host with the ping module?
Which ansible-playbook option does a dry run and reports what would change without changing anything?
In a playbook, which task correctly makes sure the nginx package is installed?
cards.back: - name: Install nginx / apt: / name: nginx / state: present (each part on its own indented line)

cards.front: Which command runs site.yml only against hosts in the web group, using inventory.ini?
What does it mean that most Ansible modules are idempotent?
cards.back: Running the same task again makes no further change once the system is in the right state

points: clone, branch, add, commit, push, then open a pull request.
git pull is git fetch plus a merge.
.gitignore keeps secrets and build files out of the repo.
git revert undoes a shared commit safely. reset rewrites history.
learn.idea: Git tracks every change to scripts and config. CI/CD pipelines test and deploy those changes automatically.
learn.memory: Add stages, commit saves, push shares.

questions.q: A developer cloned a repo, edited files and wants to save a snapshot with the message fix typo. Which sequence is correct?
questions.explain: Stage the changes with git add, then commit them. git push uploads them later.

questions.q: Which command creates a new branch named feature and switches to it?
questions.explain: checkout -b creates and switches in one step. git switch -c feature does the same.

questions.q: Which command downloads new commits from the remote and merges them into the current branch?
questions.explain: pull is fetch plus merge. fetch only downloads.

questions.q: Which file stops Git from tracking .env files and the build/ folder?
questions.explain: Patterns in .gitignore are skipped by git add. Keep secrets out of repos this way.

questions.q: A bad commit was already pushed to the shared main branch. Which command undoes it safely for everyone?
questions.explain: revert adds a new commit that undoes the change. Force-pushing a reset rewrites history other people already have.

questions.q: In a CI/CD pipeline, which part automatically builds and tests code each time a change is pushed?
questions.explain: CI builds and tests every change. Continuous deployment then releases changes that pass.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Put the steps to fix a script and propose the change in order.
steps: Edit the script and run git add
Open a pull request for review
questions.explain: Work on a branch, commit, push the branch, then ask for review before merging.

questions.q: Which command shows which files are changed, staged or untracked?
questions.explain: git status shows the working tree state. git log shows commit history.

Which command downloads new commits from the remote and merges them into the current branch?

points: Use a virtual environment per project: python3 -m venv.
pip install -r requirements.txt installs a project's dependencies.
Never paste passwords, keys or private data into a public AI tool.
Read and test AI-written code in a safe place before production.
learn.idea: Python handles automation that outgrows Bash. AI tools can help write scripts, but you check everything before it runs.
learn.memory: AI drafts, you verify.

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of Python 3?
options: It is binary compatible with Java.
questions.explain: Python 3 is open source and grows through modules and packages. It is not fully compatible with Python 2.

questions.q: Which command creates an isolated Python environment in the folder .venv?
questions.explain: The venv module creates the environment. Activate it with source .venv/bin/activate.

questions.q: Which command installs every dependency listed by a Python project?
questions.explain: -r reads package names from the file. pip freeze writes the installed list out.

questions.q: Which pip command installs the requests package inside the active virtual environment?
questions.explain: With the venv active, pip installs into it and not into the system Python.

questions.q: An AI assistant wrote a Bash script that deletes old files. What should the administrator do before running it on production servers?
options: Read it line by line and test it on a non-production system
Run it right away with sudo
Run it on production first and watch the logs
Ask the AI if the script is safe and trust the answer
questions.explain: AI output can be wrong but sound sure. Review and test it like any untrusted script.

questions.q: An admin wants help fixing a config file from a public AI chatbot. What must be removed first?
options: Passwords, API keys and other secrets in the file
questions.explain: Public AI tools may keep prompts. Strip secrets and private data, or use an approved private tool.

Which command creates an isolated Python environment in the folder .venv?
Which command installs every dependency listed by a Python project?
Which pip command installs the requests package inside the active virtual environment?

cards.back: Read it line by line and test it on a non-production system
