cards.back: Passwords, API keys and other secrets in the file

points: emergency.target gives a root shell with almost nothing mounted. rescue.target mounts local filesystems.
A bad /etc/fstab line is the most common reason for dropping to emergency mode. nofail prevents it.
rd.break on RHEL stops in the initramfs so you can reset the root password.
journalctl -b -1 shows logs from the previous boot.
learn.idea: When a system will not boot, find which stage failed: firmware, GRUB, kernel, initramfs or systemd. Each has its own fix.
learn.memory: GRUB menu, press e, edit the linux line. That is your way in.

questions.q: A system booted with a read-only root filesystem after a power loss. Which command remounts / read-write for repairs?
questions.explain: remount,rw changes the mount options without unmounting.

questions.q: Which command shows kernel ring buffer messages, including hardware found during boot?
questions.explain: dmesg prints the kernel ring buffer. journalctl -k -b gives the same messages from the journal.

questions.q: A system fails to boot normally. Which systemd target gives a root shell with no services and only the root filesystem mounted read-only?
questions.explain: emergency is the most minimal. rescue also mounts local filesystems and starts a few basic services.

questions.q: Which kernel parameter, added at the GRUB menu on RHEL, stops boot inside the initramfs so the root password can be reset?
questions.explain: rd.break drops to a shell before the real root is switched in. The real root is then at /sysroot.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Reset a forgotten root password on RHEL 9. Put the steps in order.
steps: At the GRUB menu, highlight the entry and press e
Add rd.break to the end of the linux line and boot with Ctrl+X
Run passwd root and set the new password
Run touch /.autorelabel, then exit twice to reboot
questions.explain: The autorelabel step fixes the SELinux label on /etc/shadow. Without it, logins can fail after the reset.

questions.q: After a kernel update the server panics with "VFS: Unable to mount root fs". What is the quickest way to get it running?
options: Boot the previous kernel from the GRUB menu, then rebuild the initramfs for the new one
Run fsck on every disk from the panic screen
questions.explain: The older kernel still has a working initramfs. Boot it, then fix the new kernel with dracut -f.

questions.q: A server drops to emergency mode after a USB disk listed in /etc/fstab was removed. What is the right long-term fix?
options: Remove the line or add the nofail option to that fstab entry
Set the default target to emergency.target
questions.explain: Without nofail, systemd waits for the device and fails the boot when it is missing.

questions.q: Which command shows log messages from the boot before the current one?
questions.explain: -b 0 is the current boot and -b -1 the one before. The journal must be persistent for this to work.

questions.q: Boot takes three minutes. Which command lists the units that took longest to start?
questions.explain: blame sorts units by start time. systemd-analyze critical-chain shows the slowest path.

questions.q: A server stops at a grub rescue prompt after a disk change. What is the usual fix?
options: Boot from rescue media, chroot into the system and reinstall GRUB with grub2-install
Run fsck from the grub rescue prompt
Run dracut -f from the grub rescue prompt
questions.explain: GRUB cannot find its files. Reinstall it from a live or rescue environment, then rebuild grub.cfg.

questions.q: Which kernel parameter added at the GRUB menu boots into rescue mode for one boot?
questions.explain: systemd.unit= picks the target for this boot only. The default target is not changed.

questions.q: The nofail option in /etc/fstab lets the system finish booting even if that device is missing.
questions.explain: Use it for removable or network disks that are not needed to boot.

questions.q: On RHEL, which command makes a specific installed kernel the default boot entry?
questions.explain: grubby manages boot entries on RHEL. grubby --default-kernel shows the current default.

cards.front: A system booted with a read-only root filesystem after a power loss. Which command remounts / read-write for repairs?
Which command shows kernel ring buffer messages, including hardware found during boot?
A system fails to boot normally. Which systemd target gives a root shell with no services and only the root filesystem mounted read-only?
Which kernel parameter, added at the GRUB menu on RHEL, stops boot inside the initramfs so the root password can be reset?
After a kernel update the server panics with "VFS: Unable to mount root fs". What is the quickest way to get it running?
cards.back: Boot the previous kernel from the GRUB menu, then rebuild the initramfs for the new one

cards.front: A server drops to emergency mode after a USB disk listed in /etc/fstab was removed. What is the right long-term fix?
cards.back: Remove the line or add the nofail option to that fstab entry

points: Load average higher than the CPU count (nproc) means CPU saturation.
High wa in top or iostat means the disk is the bottleneck.
Heavy swapping (si/so in vmstat) means not enough RAM.
The OOM killer leaves messages in dmesg and the journal.
learn.idea: Slow systems usually run out of CPU, memory or disk I/O. Measure first, then fix the real bottleneck.
learn.memory: Load vs nproc. wa for wait. si/so for swap.

questions.q: A Linux administrator receives reports that an application is not finishing jobs in time. Exhibit: $ uptime → load average: 7.75, 5.72, 5.17 | $ nproc → 4 | $ free -m → plenty of free memory, swap unused | $ vmstat 1 → wa 0. Which action helps speed up the jobs?
options: Increase the free memory available to the system
Increase the CPU resources available to the system
Increase the swap space available to the system
Increase the number of disks available to the system
questions.explain: A load around 7 on 4 CPUs means processes are waiting for CPU. Memory, swap and disk wait all look fine.

questions.q: Which of the following describes collecting system events from many sources into a single location?
questions.explain: Log aggregation collects logs from many hosts into one place so they can be searched together.

questions.q: Which tool reports per-disk I/O use and helps identify a storage bottleneck?
questions.explain: iostat -x shows extended stats per device, including %util and wait times.

questions.q: Which command shows the top 10 processes by CPU use in one snapshot?
questions.explain: ps sorted by CPU, descending, then head. 11 lines because the first is the header.

questions.q: Which command gives a readable summary of RAM and swap use?
questions.explain: free -h shows total, used, free, buffers and cache, and available memory, plus swap.

questions.q: Users report a slow server. Exhibit: $ free -h → Mem available 120Mi of 8Gi | Swap used 3.9Gi of 4Gi | $ vmstat 1 → si 850 so 920. What is the most likely cause?
options: The server is short of RAM and swapping heavily
questions.explain: Very little available memory plus constant swap in (si) and out (so) means memory pressure.

questions.q: A database process vanished overnight. Which command best confirms the kernel killed it for lack of memory?
questions.explain: The OOM killer logs "Out of memory: Killed process" in the kernel log.

questions.q: top shows 45.0 wa in the CPU line. What does this point to?
options: CPUs are waiting on disk I/O
The CPU is fully busy running user code
Too many users are logged in
questions.explain: wa is I/O wait time. Check iostat and iotop to find the busy disk and process.

questions.q: Which tool shows, live, which processes are doing the most disk reads and writes?
questions.explain: iotop is top for disk I/O. iftop does the same for network traffic.

questions.q: On a server with 4 CPU cores, a load average of 4.0 means the CPUs are fully used but no processes are waiting.
questions.explain: Load equal to the core count is roughly full use. Above it, processes start queuing for CPU.

questions.q: ps shows several processes in state Z that will not go away. What are they, and how are they cleared?
options: Zombie processes, cleared when their parent reaps them or the parent is restarted
Kernel threads, cleared with a reboot only
questions.explain: A zombie has already exited. Only its parent can collect its status. Fixing or restarting the parent clears it.

questions.q: A manager wants CPU use from yesterday afternoon. Which tool can report past performance data?
questions.explain: sar, from the sysstat package, reads data collected at set intervals.

questions.q: Which command lists processes sorted by memory use, highest first?
questions.explain: The minus sign sorts in descending order.

questions.q: Which kernel setting controls how willing the system is to move memory pages to swap?
questions.explain: Lower swappiness keeps more in RAM. Set it with sysctl and save it in /etc/sysctl.d/ to persist.

questions.q: A monitoring rule sends an alert when disk use on / goes above 90%. What is this called?
questions.explain: Threshold monitoring alerts when a metric crosses a set value.

questions.q: Overall CPU use looks low, but one app is slow. Which command shows use for each CPU core, to spot one core pinned at 100%?
questions.explain: mpstat -P ALL breaks usage out per core. A single-threaded app can max one core while the average looks fine.

questions.q: HOTSPOT: Match each symptom to the best first tool.
pairs: One process is using a lot of CPU
questions.explain: Pick the tool that measures the resource the symptom points to.

cards.front: Which of the following describes collecting system events from many sources into a single location?
Which tool reports per-disk I/O use and helps identify a storage bottleneck?
Which command shows the top 10 processes by CPU use in one snapshot?
Which command gives a readable summary of RAM and swap use?
A database process vanished overnight. Which command best confirms the kernel killed it for lack of memory?
top shows 45.0 wa in the CPU line. What does this point to?
cards.back: CPUs are waiting on disk I/O

points: ip link shows if the link is up. ip addr shows the address. ip route shows the gateway.
If an IP works but a name fails, it is DNS.
ss -tlnp shows what is listening and on which address.
nc and curl test a port or service directly.
learn.idea: Work from the bottom up: link, address, gateway, remote IP, then DNS and the service port.
learn.memory: Link, IP, gateway, remote, name, port.

questions.q: Which tcpdump command captures only SSH traffic on eth0 and writes it to ssh.pcap?
questions.explain: -i picks the interface, -w writes a pcap file and port 22 is the capture filter.

questions.q: Which command lists all TCP listening sockets with the process that owns each one?
questions.explain: t is TCP, l is listening, n is numeric and p shows the process.

questions.q: Which command queries DNS for www.example.com and shows the answer and the server that replied?
questions.explain: dig shows the full question and answer, the TTL and which server answered. dig +trace follows the path from the root.

questions.q: Which command shows each hop to 8.8.8.8 and keeps measuring loss and latency per hop?
questions.explain: mtr combines ping and traceroute and updates continuously.

questions.q: Users report a server is unreachable. What is the best first network test from the server itself?
questions.explain: Testing the gateway first separates local problems from upstream ones.

questions.q: Exhibit: $ ip -br a → eth0 UP 192.168.1.50/24 | $ ping -c1 192.168.1.1 → 1 received | $ ping -c1 8.8.8.8 → 1 received | $ ping google.com → Temporary failure in name resolution. What should be checked next?
options: The DNS servers in /etc/resolv.conf or resolvectl status
questions.explain: The link, address, gateway and internet all work. Only name lookups fail, so it is DNS.

questions.q: Which command checks whether TCP port 443 on 10.0.0.5 accepts connections?
questions.explain: nc -z checks the port without sending data and -v reports the result. ping does not use ports.

questions.q: Which command shows only the HTTP status line and headers from a web server?
questions.explain: -I sends a HEAD request and prints the headers, including the status code.

questions.q: Exhibit: $ ip route → 192.168.5.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel | $ ping 8.8.8.8 → connect: Network is unreachable. What is wrong?
options: The remote host is blocking ICMP
questions.explain: Only the local subnet is in the table. Add a default gateway with ip route add default via the router.

questions.q: Exhibit: $ ip link show eth0 → state DOWN. Which command brings the interface up?
questions.explain: ip link set up changes the link state. Then check that it gets an address.

questions.q: Two hosts may be using the same IP address. Which command checks for a duplicate before using 192.168.1.40?
questions.explain: arping -D does duplicate address detection. Any reply means another host already has the address.

questions.q: Small pings work over a VPN, but large file transfers hang. Which test checks for an MTU problem?
questions.explain: -M do forbids fragmentation and -s sets the size. If large sizes fail, lower the MTU.

questions.q: Exhibit: $ ss -tlnp | grep 8080 → LISTEN 127.0.0.1:8080 java. Remote users cannot reach the app. What is the fix?
options: Configure the app to listen on 0.0.0.0 or the server's IP instead of 127.0.0.1
questions.explain: 127.0.0.1 accepts only local connections. The app must bind to an external address.

questions.q: Which command scans host 10.0.0.20 for open TCP ports 1 to 1000?
questions.explain: nmap scans remote ports. Only scan systems you are allowed to test.

questions.q: A server's network is slow. Which command shows the NIC's negotiated speed and duplex?
questions.explain: A link stuck at 100 Mb/s or half duplex often points to a bad cable or a switch port mismatch.

questions.q: SIMULATION: A server cannot reach a website. Put these checks in bottom-up order.
steps: Check the link state with ip link
Check the IP address with ip addr
Ping a remote IP such as 8.8.8.8
questions.explain: Each step proves the layer below it works, so you find the broken layer quickly.

questions.q: Which command shows packet error and drop counters for each interface?
questions.explain: -s adds RX and TX statistics, including errors and drops.

points: No space left but df shows free space: check inodes with df -i.
Space not freed after deleting a log: a process still holds it open. Find it with lsof +L1.
Never run fsck on a mounted filesystem.
target is busy: find the user of the mount with lsof or fuser.
learn.idea: Storage problems show up as full disks, failing mounts or read-only filesystems. Read the exact error first.
learn.memory: df -h for blocks, df -i for inodes.

questions.q: Before running fsck on /dev/sdb1, which step is required?
questions.explain: fsck on a mounted filesystem can corrupt it. Unmount it, or use -n for a read-only check.

questions.q: Which command reads the SMART data of /dev/sda to look for signs of drive failure?
questions.explain: smartctl -a shows SMART attributes and self-test logs. badblocks -w overwrites the disk.

questions.q: Exhibit: touch: cannot touch 'file': No space left on device | $ df -h /var → 40% used | $ df -i /var → IUse% 100%. What is the cause?
options: The filesystem has run out of inodes, usually from millions of tiny files
The user has no write permission
questions.explain: Every file uses one inode. Find the folder with huge numbers of small files and clean it up.

questions.q: A 20 GB log was deleted, but df still shows the space as used. Which command finds the process holding it?
questions.explain: lsof +L1 lists open files with no links left, meaning deleted but still open. Restart that process to free the space.

questions.q: Which command shows which folders under /var use the most space, sorted by size?
questions.explain: du totals each folder and sort -h orders human-readable sizes.

questions.q: An XFS filesystem reports corruption. It has been unmounted. Which command repairs it?
questions.explain: XFS has its own repair tool. The e2fsck family is for ext filesystems.

questions.q: dmesg shows "EXT4-fs error ... Remounting filesystem read-only". What should be done?
options: Stop writes, unmount the filesystem and run e2fsck, then check the disk health
Remount it read-write and keep working
questions.explain: The kernel made it read-only to protect the data. Repair it offline and check SMART for a failing disk.

questions.q: mount -t cifs fails with an error saying a helper program may be needed. What is the likely fix?
questions.explain: Mounting SMB shares needs mount.cifs from cifs-utils. NFS needs nfs-utils.

questions.q: /proc/mdstat shows md0 degraded with /dev/sdc marked failed. A new disk /dev/sdd is installed. Which command adds it so the array rebuilds?
questions.explain: --add puts the new disk in the array and the rebuild starts. Remove the failed disk with --remove first.

questions.q: umount /data fails with "target is busy". Which command shows what is using it?
questions.explain: fuser -m lists processes using the mount. lsof +D /data also works. A shell sitting inside the folder counts too.

questions.q: Exhibit: $ smartctl -A /dev/sdb → Reallocated_Sector_Ct 1 last week, 212 today. What should the administrator do?
options: Back up the data and replace the disk soon
Run fsck every day to fix the sectors
Format the disk to reset the counter
Ignore it, since the disk still works
questions.explain: A fast-rising reallocated sector count means the drive is failing. Get the data off first.

questions.q: HOTSPOT: Match each storage error to the best fix.
pairs: No space left, but df -h shows free space
Find users with lsof or fuser
Run e2fsck with a backup superblock
Space not freed after deleting a large log
Restart the process holding it open
questions.explain: Each message points to a different cause, so read it closely before acting.

questions.q: An administrator wants to watch an Apache error.log in real time and also save what appears to another file for later. Which command does this?
questions.explain: tee writes to the file and to the screen at the same time. Plain redirection hides the output.

questions.q: On a RHEL 9 server that keeps logs only in the systemd journal, which command shows new log entries live?
questions.explain: journalctl -f follows the journal. /var/log/syslog is a Debian-family file, and dmesg shows only kernel messages.

questions.q: Running ./run.sh gives Permission denied. Exhibit: $ ls -l run.sh → -rw-r--r-- 1 ops ops 412 run.sh. What fixes it?
questions.explain: The file has no execute bit. Add it, or run it with bash run.sh.

questions.q: A web page returns 403 Forbidden. File permissions are 644 and the owner is correct. SELinux is enforcing. What is the most likely fix?
questions.explain: Files moved from a home folder keep the wrong SELinux type. restorecon gives them httpd_sys_content_t.

questions.q: A user gets "is not in the sudoers file. This incident will be reported." on RHEL. How should admin rights be granted?
options: Add the user to the wheel group with usermod -aG wheel username
Give the user the root password
questions.explain: On RHEL the wheel group has sudo rights. On Debian and Ubuntu the group is sudo.

questions.q: A service will not start after a config change. What should the administrator check first?
options: systemctl status app and journalctl -u app
questions.explain: The status output and unit logs usually name the exact error and line.

questions.q: Exhibit: $ systemctl status nginx → bind() to 0.0.0.0:80 failed (98: Address already in use). Which command finds the cause?
questions.explain: Another process already listens on port 80. ss -tlnp shows which one.

questions.q: A script copied from a Windows PC fails with "/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter". What fixes it?
options: Convert the line endings with dos2unix script.sh
questions.explain: Windows line endings add a carriage return (^M) to every line. dos2unix or sed -i 's/\r$//' removes it.

questions.q: The user bob is locked out after too many failed logins. Which command clears the pam_faillock counter?
questions.explain: faillock --reset clears the failure count kept by pam_faillock. passwd -u unlocks a password lock, which is a separate thing.

questions.q: A script works when run by hand but fails from cron with "command not found". What is the most likely cause?
options: cron runs with a short PATH, so the script needs full command paths or its own PATH line
questions.explain: cron's environment is minimal. Set PATH at the top of the crontab or use full paths like /usr/bin/rsync.

questions.q: An app fails with "Too many open files". Which change fixes it for a systemd service?
options: Raise LimitNOFILE in the service's unit (or drop-in) and restart it
Run chmod -R 777 on the app folder
questions.explain: The open file limit is per process. For systemd services set LimitNOFILE. For shell sessions use ulimit -n.

questions.q: SIMULATION: The app service failed after an update. Put the troubleshooting steps in order.
steps: Check the state with systemctl status app
Read the logs with journalctl -u app
Fix the config error the logs point to
Restart the service with systemctl restart app
Confirm it is listening with ss -tlnp
questions.explain: Find the error, fix it, restart, then prove it works from the outside view.
